claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite tends to undergo phase separation and form interfacial voids under service conditions.
Approximately 5 wt% nanoscale TiC can be uniformly dispersed in the W–Cu composite, particularly at W–Cu interfaces.
TiC particles localize at grain boundaries and interfacial regions.
Dispersed TiC particles act as mechanical stabilizers by strengthening boundaries and resisting their migration at elevated temperature.
TiC particles act as diffusion barriers at W–Cu interfaces.
TiC restricts atomic diffusion and migration at W–Cu interfaces under combined thermal and irradiation stresses.
Restricted interfacial diffusion and migration suppress phase-separated regions and interfacial void formation in W–Cu.
Stabilizing the W–Cu interface maintains a continuous heat-transfer pathway.
TiC-modified W–Cu will have fewer interfacial voids than untreated W–Cu under identical heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
TiC-modified W–Cu will have greater microstructural stability than untreated W–Cu under identical service conditions.
TiC-modified W–Cu will retain a higher and more stable thermal conductivity than untreated W–Cu.
Interfacial voids and phase-separated regions degrade the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu during high-heat-flux and irradiation exposure.
The effective TiC-content regime is approximately 3–10 wt%.
The intervention applies under high heat flux and neutron/gamma irradiation relevant to W-based plasma-facing material and Cu-based cooling-component joints.
A W-based composite with uniformly distributed TiC can withstand heat flux as high as 200 MW/m², nearly twice that sustained by pure W.
TiC additions to W-based materials increase recrystallization temperature and irradiation resistance.
